Senses.Explanation: The buddhas of the three times do not know it, but cats and white oxen do reverses the expected hierarchy of knowing. A lamp preserves Nanquan's saying inside Dawei's explicit quotation, after which Dawei challenges both sides of the contrast. In the stronger Ancient Venerables record, Cuiyan states the same contrast in his own hall address, raises the whisk, and says the cats and white oxen are there radiating light and shaking the earth. These are distinct deployments, not parallel recensions.

Occurrences.Kwic: 家村裏賣卜東卜西卜忽然卜著也不定僧便問忽然卜著時如何師云伏惟。師云大用現前不存軌則僧便問如何是大用現前師乃拈拄杖高聲唱云釋迦老子來也有時以拄杖打火鑪一下大眾眼目定動師乃云火鑪㪍跳上三十三天見麼見麼眾無語師云無智人前莫說打你頭破百裂。師云看看法身變作燈籠超佛越祖之談從你󷗿跟下過也僧云󷗿跟下認得時如何師云鈍置殺我僧云與麼則逈然不在者裏也師云十萬八千。舉槃山語云光境俱忘復
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (C/C077/C077n1710.xml). Recorded Sayings of Ancient Masters (古尊宿語錄). Speaker: Yunmen Wenyan.

Occurrences.Kwic: 門道：弟子請益。門云：目前無異草。師云：世界闊一尺，古鏡闊一尺。不信道：誰知席帽下，元是昔愁人？雲藏谷口，水注滄溟，萬法本然，而人自閙。於此之外，復且如何？拈拄杖，云：拄杖子𨁝跳上三十三天，築著帝釋鼻孔，地神惡發奏與空神，空神奏上天神，如今却在上藍手中。諸人還見麼？若也見去，隨方毗尼；若也不會，一任𨁝跳。舉：調達謗佛，生身陷地獄。佛令阿難傳旨：汝在獄中安否？達云：我

Occurrences.Kwic: 門云：扇子𨁝跳上三十三天，築著帝釋鼻孔，把東海鯉魚打一棒，雨似盆傾。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (X/X71/X71n1420.xml). Chushi Fanqi: Sayings (楚石梵琦禪師語錄). Speaker: Yunmen Wenyan.

Senses.Explanation: The Heaven of the Thirty-Three is the celestial realm ruled by Shakra and used in Chan hyperbole as a reachable height. The preceding instruction says that such things are ordinary fare before a monastic, who must sit in a thicket of thorns as the great site of awakening and recognize what one originally is amid mixing with mud and water. After asking how it can be seen, the instruction marks a raised staff and warns that even seeing it does not escape that staff. A following hall address says that, when feelings of sacred and ordinary are exhausted, true constancy stands exposed; the raised fly whisk then leaps to the Heaven of the Thirty-Three and tweaks Shakra’s nose. The image dramatizes unrestricted movement rather than literal travel advice.

Entries.SourceTerm: 三十年弄馬伎。今日却被驢撲

Senses.PreferredTarget: thirty years showing horse tricks, today thrown by a donkey
AlternateTargets: thirty years playing horseman, only to be thrown by a donkey today
SearchAliases: thirty years playing horseman, only to be thrown by a donkey today
Senses.Note: The animals mark the reversal in this exchange, not a general hierarchy of mounts.

Occurrences.Kwic: 山前有古寺基。諗曰。和尚自住取。後到師處。師曰。老老大大漢何不住去。諗曰。什麼處住得。師曰。老老大大漢住處也不知。諗曰。三十年弄馬伎。今日却被驢撲眾僧侍立。師曰。只恁麼白立無箇說處一場氣悶。有僧擬出問。師乃打之。曰為眾竭力。便入方丈。有行者參師曰。曾去看趙州麼。曰和

The seasoned horse-handler is unexpectedly thrown by the humbler donkey: Zhaozhou marks that the exchange has caught him.

Senses.Note: The interval remains literal future time. Its recurring Chan job is to defer how a saying, encounter, or person will be judged, remembered, or repeated.

Occurrences.Kwic: 且道。把住好放行好。三十年後逢人不得錯舉。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (T/T47/T47n1997.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Yuanwu Foguo. Yuanwu Keqin asks whether holding fast or letting go is better and warns the assembly not to repeat it wrongly thirty years later.

Occurrences.Kwic: 僧喝一喝云。三十年後大有人笑在。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (T/T47/T47n1998A.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Dahui Pujue. An unnamed monk gives a shout and predicts that many people will laugh thirty years later; Dahui Zonggao answers him in the following turn.

ActorAttribution.GrammarEvidence: 僧喝一喝云 explicitly introduces the monk's exact headword-bearing forecast; the following 師云 begins Dahui Zonggao's reply.

Occurrences.Kwic: 畢竟在什麼處。三十年後。待山僧換骨出來。却向爾道。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (T/T48/T48n2003.xml). Blue Cliff Record by Chan Master Yuanwu Foguo. Yuanwu Keqin asks where the matter finally lies and says he will tell the reader after this mountain monk changes his bones thirty years later.

Occurrences.Kwic: 師云：去聖時遙，人多懈怠，三十年後討箇師僧也難得。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (X/X79/X79n1557.xml). Essential Compendium of the United Lamp. Nanyang Huizhong says that with the sages remote and people lax, thirty years later even finding a genuine monk will be difficult.

Occurrences.Kwic: 師云：這箇因緣，三十年後擲地作金聲。仰云：須是和尚提唱始得。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (X/X79/X79n1557.xml). Essential Compendium of the United Lamp. Guishan Lingyou says that this encounter will strike the ground with a golden ring thirty years later; Yangshan Huiji answers that Guishan must proclaim it.

Occurrences.Kwic: 問靈山一會何異今日。師曰。莫妄想。僧云。作家宗師。師曰。三十年後自有人知。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (T/T51/T51n2077.xml). Continued Record of the Transmission of the Lamp. Kaixian Shanxian answers that thirty years later someone will know, after a monk calls him an accomplished lineage master.

Occurrences.Kwic: 且道衲僧據箇甚麼？良久曰：三十年後莫孤負人。卓拄杖，下座。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (X/X82/X82n1571.xml). Complete Five Lamps (Vols. 34–120). Chengxin Shengzong asks what patch-robed monks rely on, pauses, and warns them not to fail him thirty years later.

Occurrences.Kwic: 僧拍手一下便出。師云。三十年後悟去在。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (T/T47/T47n1998A.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Dahui Pujue. After a monk claps and leaves, Dahui Zonggao says that he will understand thirty years later.

Senses.Explanation: Thirty years later is ordinary future time turned into a recurring public reckoning: the Chan records use it to forecast how a saying, encounter, or person will be laughed at, understood, repeated, or misreported. Yuanwu Keqin warns his assembly not to repeat his holding-fast and letting-go question wrongly thirty years later; elsewhere he postpones an answer until this mountain monk has changed his bones. When a monk predicts that people will laugh in thirty years, Dahui Zonggao immediately asks why wait and says people already laugh. Nanyang Huizhong predicts that a genuine monk will be hard to find, Guishan Lingyou says an encounter will later ring when struck, and Kaixian Shanxian says future people will know. Chengxin Shengzong's warning not to fail him later keeps the expression a forecast and test, not an instruction to wait a prescribed interval.

Senses.Note: Eight works attest the fixed count as an assigned, threatened, deserved, retrospectively imposed, or ironically remitted beating.

Occurrences.Kwic: 諸人未跨法堂門，脚跟下好與三十棒。

Kaixian Zhi owns the complete headword-bearing turn.

Occurrences.Kwic: 未踏船舷時好與三十棒也
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (D/D48/D48n8939.xml). Recorded Sayings of Ancient Venerable Masters (古尊宿語錄): Dahui Zonggao is the exact headword speaker. Occurrences.Kwic: 三十棒一棒也放他不過。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (X/X66/X66n1297.xml). Dharma Grove of the Tradition’s Mirror (宗鑑法林): Fohri Xi is the exact headword speaker.  Fohri Xi says that of thirty blows not even one could be spared the two earlier commentators. Fohri Xi owns the complete headword-bearing turn.

Occurrences.Kwic: 山僧今日有三十棒要世尊喫
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (X/X66/X66n1296.xml). Compilation of the School Gate’s “Raising Old Cases” (宗門拈古彙集): Nanjian Wen is the exact headword speaker. Nanjian says he has thirty blows for the World-Honored One to take today. Nanjian Wen owns the complete headword-bearing turn.

Occurrences.Kwic: 師曰：放你三十棒。

Strict Lineage of the Five Lamps (Vols. 10–25) (五燈嚴統(第10卷-第25卷)): Jian Shan is the exact headword speaker. after an unnamed monk requests expedient help, Jian Shan says, “I let you off with thirty blows.” Jian Shan owns the complete headword-bearing turn.

Occurrences.Kwic: 莫動著，動著三十棒
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (X/X84/X84n1583.xml). Orthodox Continuation of the Lamp (續燈正統): Baoning Renyong is the exact headword speaker. Baoning’s hall address: he says not to move; move and it is thirty blows. Baoning Renyong owns the complete headword-bearing turn.

Occurrences.Kwic: 師見僧乃曰。見成公案。放汝三十棒。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (X/X80/X80n1565.xml). Five Lamps Compendium (五燈會元): Qingxi Hongjin is the exact headword speaker. Five Lamps Compendium (五燈會元): on seeing a monk, Qingxi calls it a ready-made public case and lets him off with thirty blows. Qingxi Hongjin owns the complete headword-bearing turn.

Occurrences.Kwic: 未到曹溪時，與汝三十棒了也。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (X/X79/X79n1557.xml). Essential Compendium of the United Lamp (聯燈會要): Xuedou Chongxian is the exact headword speaker. Xuedou substitutes the patriarch’s verdict, “before you reached Caoxi I had already given you thirty blows.” Xuedou Chongxian owns the complete headword-bearing turn.

Senses.Explanation: Thirty blows is a fixed counted beating assigned as a public verdict in Chan encounters and later comments. The sentence can arrive before action: Kaixian says it is due before crossing the teaching-hall gate, Dahui quotes its being due before stepping onto a boat, and Baoning makes movement itself incur it. It can also be retrospective or directed upward: Xuedou assigns it before Huineng reaches Caoxi, Nanjian has thirty blows for the World-Honored One, and Fohri Xi refuses to spare even one blow from earlier commentators. “I let you off with thirty blows” makes the sentence itself a pointed form of leniency in Jian Shan and Qingxi. Zen bends a conventional counted beating into a reusable teaching-seat judgement whose recipient may be monk, commentator, patriarch, or buddha.

Entries.SourceTerm: 三千劍客今何在、獨許莊周致太平

Senses.PreferredTarget: where are the three thousand swordsmen now? Only Zhuang Zhou is permitted to bring about great peace
AlternateTargets: the three thousand swordsmen are gone; Zhuang Zhou alone is allowed to make peace
Senses.Note: The two retained sermons are independent uses.

Occurrences.Kwic: 禪師。婺州姜氏子。上堂拈拄杖曰。還見麼。窮諸玄辯。若一毫置於太虛竭世樞機。似一滴投於巨壑。德山老人雖則焚其疏鈔。也是賊過後張弓。且道文彩未彰以前。又作麼生理論。三千劍客今何在。獨許莊周致太平上堂。種田博飯地藏家風。客來喫茶趙州禮度。且道護聖門下別有甚麼長處。良久曰。尋常不放山泉出。屋底清池吟照人。化士出問。促

Occurrences.VariantForm: 三千劍客今何在。獨許莊周致太平

Occurrences.Kwic: 不見毘耶離城。彼上人一室。寥寥是何物。師召大眾云。高著眼。便下座。上堂云。黃金為地白銀為壁。釋迦老子不合向者裏屙。師以拄杖撥一下云。看看。落爾諸人頭上。上堂云。三千劍客今何在。獨許莊周致太平。便下座。一日云。大眾。者一片田地。分付來多時也。爾諸人四至界畔。猶未識在。若要中心一樹子。我也不惜。良久云。放憨作麼。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (T/T47/T47n1996.xml). Mingjue Sayings (明覺禪師語錄). Speaker: Xuedou Chongxian.
Occurrences.VariantForm: 三千劍客今何在。獨許莊周致太平

Senses.Explanation: Daochang Yougui asks where the three thousand swordsmen have gone and permits only Zhuang Zhou to bring about great peace. Xuedou Chongxian gives the same couplet as an entire address and leaves the seat. The Extended Lamp Record places the line in Yougui's address after he raises his staff; Xuedou's own later record preserves his separate delivery.

Senses.Note: This is a conventional nested cosmological unit, not merely a count of three thousand separate worlds.

Occurrences.Kwic: 謂若有人。能善攝化三千大千世界中遍滿眾生。皆悉無餘。令行十善
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source writing (T/T48/T48n2016.xml). Record of the Mirror of the School. Author: Yongming Yanshou uses the technical world-system as the full scope filled by beings.

Senses.Explanation: The term names the conventional nested world-system known as a great chiliocosm. Yongming Yanshou asks the reader to imagine someone guiding every being filling this entire world-system, with none omitted, into the ten wholesome actions. The construction treats the phrase as one scale unit, not a simple numeral modifying worlds.

Senses.PreferredTarget: few people know the three-way crossroads
AlternateTargets: at the three-forked road, few know
SearchAliases: at the three-forked road, few know
Senses.Note: The saying is one direct answer in Xutang’s record and remains provisional.

Occurrences.Kwic: 南來。殿閣生微涼。又作麼生。師云。也不較多。僧云。大慧聞得便悟去。又作麼生。師云。𢬵箇渾身入地獄。僧云。今日忽有人。問和尚如何是諸佛出身處。未審如何答他。師云。三叉路口少人知。僧禮拜。云謝師答話。師云。椎空聽響。師乃云。財法二施。等無差別。因甚北路山高。南路山低。會得一句子。如沾甘露毛骨頓清。投得一箸子。如飲醍醐。群心飽德徑山傍若無
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (T/T47/T47n2000.xml). Recorded Sayings of Monk Xutang (虛堂和尚語錄). Speaker: Xutang Zhiyu.

Senses.Explanation: Xutang Zhiyu answers “where do buddhas emerge?” with the little-known three-way crossroads. Xutang’s questioner has already compared Yunmen’s “East Mountain walks on the water” and Yuanwu’s south-wind line. When he asks how Xutang himself would answer, Xutang gives the crossroads and then rejects the questioner’s thanks as striking emptiness and listening for an echo.

Senses.Note: This is the structural sense only. It must not be used to erase the distinct named configurations stored as separate senses.

Occurrences.Kwic: 或一言唱道，或三句敷揚，或善巧應機，遂成多義。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (X/X82/X82n1571.xml). Complete Five Lamps (Vols. 34–120) (五燈全書(第34卷-第120卷)): Shanquan Huitai owns the exact headword-bearing wording in the complete source unit.

Senses.Explanation: Three phrases can simply mean words arranged as a set of three. Shanquan Huitai lists speaking a single word, setting forth three phrases, and responding skillfully to the occasion as different ways that multiple meanings arise. The numbered form does not by itself identify one fixed Chan teaching: Baizhang Huaihai, Wuzhu, Fenyang Shanzhao, Yunmen Wenyan, and Linji Yixuan are associated with different triads, separated below because their members and referents differ.

Senses.PreferredTarget: Baizhang's three phrases on attachment and non-attachment
Senses.Note: The sense is master-specific because the corpus supplies a stable, separately constituted Baizhang set, not merely a different reading of an unspecified triad.

Occurrences.Kwic: 若透得三句過不被三叚管
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (C/C077/C077n1710.xml). Recorded Sayings of Ancient Venerable Masters (古尊宿語錄): Baizhang Huaihai owns the exact headword-bearing wording in the complete source unit.

Occurrences.Kwic: 昔日，百丈大師謂：祇要透得三句，第一句不得於境上取著、第二句不得住於不著、第
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (X/X72/X72n1437.xml). Expanded Record of Chan Master Yongjue Yuanxian (永覺元賢禪師廣錄): Baizhang Huaihai owns the exact headword-bearing wording in the complete source unit.

Senses.Explanation: Baizhang Huaihai's three phrases form a particular three-part statement about attachment. His record distinguishes not taking hold of objects, not dwelling in non-attachment, and not constructing an understanding of that non-dwelling and non-attachment; passing through the three phrases is then named as a further test. Yongjue Yuanxian later reproduces the same three members as Baizhang's formulation. This is a different referent from the triads associated with Wuzhu, Fenyang, Yunmen, or Linji.

Senses.PreferredTarget: Wuzhu's three-phrase teaching: no recollection, no thought, no delusion
SearchAliases: no recollection no thought no delusion
Senses.Note: The exact headword occurs in Du Hongjian's personally named question, so the occurrence records him as the non-master questioner and Wuzhu as respondent and section subject.

Occurrences.Kwic: 公問曰。弟子聞今和尚說無憶．無念．莫妄三句法門。是否。

ActorAttribution.GrammarEvidence: The section names Du Hongjian, and 公問曰 marks his question to Wuzhu.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (X/X80/X80n1565.xml). Five Lamps Compendium (五燈會元): Du Hongjian is the named non-master questioner who owns the exact headword-bearing wording.

Senses.Explanation: Wuzhu's three-phrase teaching names a fixed set: no recollection, no thought, and no delusion. In the public exchange, the official Du Hongjian asks Wuzhu whether this is the teaching he gives. Wuzhu confirms it, maps the members to precepts, concentration, and wisdom, and refuses to make the set either simply one or simply three. The entry reports that recorded configuration without importing an outside account of what its members mean.

Senses.PreferredTarget: Fenyang's three phrases: exertion, turning, and intimacy
AlternateTargets: the exerting-strength, turning-body, and intimate phrases
Senses.Note: The PreferredTarget identifies the members so a reader can distinguish this sense from the other named triads without opening the explanation.

Occurrences.Kwic: 又云。若人會得此三句。已辨三玄。更有三要語在。切須薦取。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (T/T48/T48n2006.xml). Eyes of Humans and Devas (人天眼目): Fenyang Shanzhao owns the exact headword-bearing wording in the complete source unit.

Occurrences.Kwic: 汾陽三句，如大火聚，近之不得，背之非火。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (X/X72/X72n1437.xml). Expanded Record of Chan Master Yongjue Yuanxian (永覺元賢禪師廣錄): Yongjue Yuanxian owns the exact headword-bearing wording in the complete source unit.

Senses.Explanation: Fenyang Shanzhao's three phrases are separately named for a student's exerting strength, turning the body, and intimacy. Fenyang answers a question on each member and then says that understanding these three phrases distinguishes the three mysteries while three essentials still remain. Yongjue Yuanxian later calls Fenyang's set a mass of fire that cannot be approached yet is not other than fire when turned away from. These statements identify a named Fenyang configuration rather than a generic three-part form.

Senses.Explanation: The three-inch tongue is the speaking organ in cutting and silencing formulas, while ordinary “three inches” remains a separate measure. The three-inch tongue is the speaking organ, often shortened in Chan exchanges to just 'the three inches.' Baoning Renyong supplies the full form: 'I have one mouth, containing a three-inch tongue; the teeth are all complete, and there is no right and wrong it does not speak' (我有一張口，內含三寸舌。牙齒總完全，是非無不說). An unnamed questioner asks Cuiyan Lingcan to speak 'without borrowing the three inches' (不借三寸，請師道), and another unnamed questioner calls Dahui Zonggao's 'three inches' tightly guarded (老和尚三寸甚密). The omitted noun is recoverable from the explicit full form and from the predicates of speaking. The Zen bend is this use of an ordinary measure as public shorthand for the tongue, not a claim that every occurrence of three inches names speech.

AlternateTargets: three inches in distance or thickness
Senses.Note: The fishing construction is not reassigned to the tongue merely because speech follows it. Conversely, face-skin and breath supply their own measured nouns and do not create new bare-headword meanings. The separately retained tongue sense is supported by genuine noun omission in bare public-interview uses.

Senses.Explanation: This separate sense names three inches, not the three-inch tongue. Three inches is a measure whose object and dimension are supplied by its construction. In the Boatman's case, Chuanzi Decheng says, 'the line hangs a thousand feet, its intent in the deep pool; three inches from the hook, why do you not speak?' (垂絲千尺，意在深潭，離鉤三寸，子何不道). Zhang Shangying's verse preserves the same distance from the hook. Fozhao Deguang uses the measure for thickness when he says Huangbo's facial skin remains three inches thick (面皮厚三寸). Tianru Weize's mortality warning applies the same small-span image to breath: 'when the three-inch breath is cut off, one fire burns through' (三寸氣斷，一火洞然). Distance, thickness, and the measured-breath image differ in what is measured, not in the lexical value of three inches; they therefore remain one sense rather than three context-driven senses.

Senses.Note: One referent covers both breath ending and breath prolonged.

Senses.Explanation: Three coins to buy straw sandals is the small traveling allowance attached to a plain meal or handed out as a dismissal. Chan masters place it after “eat the customary cakes,” give the three coins to a questioner, and use the line as a compact send-off after an answer has run its course. Yunfeng Wenyue says that if nobody can supply the requested sentence, eating the customary cakes will still earn three coins for straw sandals. Muting Pufu gives the phrase directly to his questioner after that questioner thanks him for instruction. Senses.Explanation: Collected absorption names a collected or absorbed mode, most often inside a specifying compound. Huineng defines the single-conduct form as carrying one straight mind while walking, standing, sitting, and lying down; he explicitly rejects defining it as sitting motionless with thought suppressed. Mazu says the ocean-seal form gathers all things as streams return to the sea, and describes dressing, eating, speaking, responding, and using the senses as occurring within the nature-of-things form. Xuansha Shibei calls the buddhas people's own-reception form and says it is never absent in walking, standing, sitting, or lying down. The compounds supply their own qualifications, so the bare headword does not reduce them all to one formula.

Donglin Guzhi warns the assembly not to build an understanding by depending on the place beneath three rafters and before the seven-foot platform. Miyun Yuanwu locates blows, sleep, and sitting there. Zhufeng Zhenxu tells monks there to watch their footing and eyebrows, while Shuzhong Wuyun permits lying down, eating, and drinking there but warns that retained measures incur a later food debt. The institutional sitting-place is one thing across these uses.

Senses.Explanation: In one transmitted public case, the contrast separates verbal ease from lived execution. Niaoke Daolin answers Bai Juyi’s objection that even a child can state the rule by saying that an eighty-year-old still cannot carry it out. Four works preserve this same Niaoke Daolin–Bai Juyi exchange rather than four separate uses. Niaoke first gives the plain rule “do no evil; carry out every good.” Bai Juyi calls it childishly easy to say; Daolin answers by opposing that verbal ease to the difficulty of an elder actually doing it.

Senses.Explanation: The three realms are only mind (三界唯心) is a received statement that Zen records quote, assert, and test in public exchanges. Yongming Yanshou quotes a document for it rather than claiming its words as his own. Mazu Daoyi states it before saying that the many appearances bear one stamp and that seeing form is seeing mind. Xuansha Shibei asks Luohan Guichen how he understands the line; Guichen points to a chair, and both call it wood. Luohan Guichen tells Fayan Wenyi that Fayan habitually repeats the paired saying, points to a courtyard stone, and asks whether the stone is inside or outside mind. Baoning Renyong follows it with clouds, rain, stream water, and flowers and demands that his listeners investigate their source. Yuanwu Keqin later raises the saying and discusses the senses. The records thus turn a received proposition into chair, stone, and landscape tests.

Senses.Explanation: Xuansha Shibei's fixed case of three people: one blind, one deaf, and one unable to speak. His recorded challenge says that the blind person cannot see a raised mallet or whisk, the deaf person cannot hear spoken complete command, and the mute person cannot answer. Xuansha asks how elders claiming to receive people would receive them. The case record then has an unnamed participant ask permission to discuss the three, depart, and receive Xuansha's double rejection; Luohan Guichen turns the question onto Xuansha, who withdraws. Yunmen Wenyan later has a questioner bow, tests his movement, hearing, and answer, and the record reports a response. The exact phrase becomes portable case language: Yuanwu Keqin raises it in the Blue Cliff Record; Liao'an Qingyu raises the Yunmen handling; Yeweng Bo tells his visible assembly that they do not have the three impairments; and Tiantai Deshao answers a direct question with “you have just asked it.” Zen bends a medical triad into Xuansha's named public-interview case about receiving people when ordinary seeing, hearing, and answering are unavailable. The entry records the moves without supplying an unstated solution.

Strict Lineage of the Five Lamps (Vols. 10–25) (五燈嚴統(第10卷-第25卷)): The Strict Lineage of the Five Lamps, volumes 10–25 (五燈嚴統(第10卷-第25卷)) records Yunmen Wenyan supplying 'one arrow pierces three checkpoints' as his own answer after the assembly gives no answer.

Senses.Explanation: A set of three tests, barriers, or checkpoint sayings, without one universal list. Wansong explicitly says that the label includes sets associated with Baizhang, Dayang, Puan, Linji, Xuansha, and the Old Pagoda master, and is not confined to Doushuai and Huanglong. In the separate formula 'one arrow pierces three checkpoints' (一鏃破三關), Qinshan is questioned about piercing three barriers and Yunmen supplies the same line as an answer after his assembly gives no answer. These are generic countable barriers; the two recurrent named taxonomies are separated below because their three questions refer to different things.

Senses.Explanation: Huanglong Huinan's named three checkpoints are a fixed set of three questions: 'How is my hand like a buddha's hand?' (我手何似佛手), 'How is my foot like a donkey's foot?' (我脚何似驢脚), and 'Where is your birth-circumstance?' (上座生緣在何處). His governing section says that the Zen community called these 'Huanglong's three checkpoints' (黃龍三關). A later hall address quotes the three questions and appraises 'Huanglong's three checkpoints' as resembling Lord Shang's institution of laws. The name therefore refers to Huanglong's particular three-question set, not to Doushuai's different list.

Senses.Explanation: Doushuai Congyue's three checkpoint sayings are a different fixed set. The first asks where one's nature is now when one parts the grass and looks to the wind only to see nature; the second asks how one escapes birth and death when the light of the eyes falls to the ground; the third asks where one goes when the four elements separate. Doushuai's record calls them 'three checkpoint sayings' (三關語) set up in the chamber to test students. A later public exchange invokes 'Doushuai's three-checkpoint sayings' and receives the invitation 'ask them one by one.' Their enumerated referents differ from Huanglong's buddha-hand, donkey-foot, and birth-circumstance questions.

Occurrences.Kwic: 南禪師信之，玉山人，族章氏。童齠深沈，年十一去家，師事定水智鑾。嘗侍鑾行次，見祠廟輒杖擊而往。十九落髮受具，遠游至廬山，依歸宗寶、棲賢諟。逾三秋，渡淮謁三角澄。久之，分座雲峰悅禪師，勉趨石霜。至中道，聞石霜不事事，因寓福嚴。時賢禪師命典記室。賢歸寂，適慈明繼席，師出迎之，悚然。及聞其說法，乃貶剝諸方，盡為邪解，皆師歷參所契證者。遂幡然曰：大丈夫心膂之間，豈可自為疑礙？造室求發藥，明揖坐，師固辭哀懇。明曰：書記參雲門禪，必善其旨。如放洞山三頓棒，是合喫不合喫？云：合喫。曰：吾始疑不堪汝師，今乃可使拜之。復曰：洞山三頓棒即且置，那裏是趙州勘破婆子處？師擬對，明擊其口。師大悟，述偈呈之。留月餘辭去，時年三十五。初住同安，次擢歸宗、黃檗、黃龍，得大法者七十有九人。然在積翠庵所接者，多衲子趨風，相與交武，竭蹙于道。初受請日，三角遣僧來審，師提唱之語有曰：智海無性，因覺妄而成凡；覺妄元虗，即凡心而見佛。便爾休去，將謂同安無折合，隨汝顛倒所欲，南斗七，北斗八。僧歸舉似澄，澄不懌。俄聞開堂

Senses.Explanation: The Jiazhou expression names the great image there, not an elephant: the records also write it as the great image, stone image, stone buddha, and great buddha of Jiazhou. Chengtian Cique calls the great buddha at Jiazhou something carved by the ancients. Huqiu Shaolong, Mi'an Xianjie, Sanjiao Zhisong, Guxue Zhenzhe, and Yezhu Fuhui retain the older spelling while repeatedly pairing the image with the iron ox of Shanzhou. Those later sayings make the image ride, eat salt, chant, or get swallowed. These are predicates assigned to the established stock figure; the graphic variants prevent reading the final graph here as a zoological elephant.

Zen what connection does that have?
Senses.Explanation: In public interviews it rejects a proposed connection. In Cuifeng Chongxian's exchange, the conclusion "then the former Zhimen is today's master" receives his answer, "what connection does that have?" (有什麼交涉). The phrase also appears in prose criticism. The Blue Cliff Record says that treating Mazu's left and right eyes as the sun-face and moon-face has "what connection?" and that such readers have missed the old matter. Elsewhere Juehua Puzhao asks, "if lips, voice, and appearances are taken as oneself, what connection does that have?" (若以唇吻聲色以為自己，有什麼交涉). In another exchange, an unnamed monk himself uses the question after the answer "the graph 'by means of'" (以字), and receives "the graph 'eight'" (八字), a spoken play on similar-sounding graph names. Zen bends an ordinary request for relevance into a compact interview verdict: the reply or explanation offered has not connected with the exchange.

Senses.Explanation: What has that to do with it? is a spoken Chan rejection of a proposed connection. The records place the question after a quotation, classification, or offered formulation and use it to deny that the proposal reaches the matter under examination. Sanshan Denglai rejects both commentary on an old exchange and inert long-bench sitting with the same question. Baiyu Jingsi dismisses a polished account of mind and teaching before setting his staff against it. Yuan'an Liao uses the question twice against stock answers offered for the study-eye and the grounded statement. Hengchuan Rugong applies it first to verbal presentation itself and later to the old moon-viewing exchange, where the masters' displayed answers are said to have nothing to do with the moon.

Senses.Explanation: Having a head but no tail is a verdict that something begins but fails to carry through to an ending. Baoning Mao applies it to Kashyapa’s handling of a case. Xuedou Chongxian calls two case figures ‘men with heads but no tails,’ and Yuanwu Keqin says that an unnamed monk’s handling is initially impressive but ends incompletely. Tianyi Yihuai gives the same verdict after an unnamed monk asks, shouts, and bows. Yangshan Huiji predicts that Linji Yixuan will have a helper who has a head but no tail, immediately expanding the phrase as ‘a beginning but no end.’ The records use the image to judge incomplete handling rather than physical deformity.

Senses.Explanation: The expression denotes one's eyebrows fall out in these Chan records. Its wording is the eyebrows (眉毛) fall out (墮落). In the corpus, the phrase is well attested. The wider family includes "the eyebrows fall" (眉毛落, 48 occurrences), "are the eyebrows still there?" (眉毛在麼, 79), and "the eyebrows become tangled together" (眉毛廝結, 129). Chan records use the loss of eyebrows as a stated consequence or accusation attached to handling Buddhist or Chan speech: one comment says that making a Buddhist teaching-discussion of a line "implicates Shimen, whose eyebrows fall out" (若作佛法商量，累他石門眉毛墮落); another points to "the place where Cuiyan's eyebrows fall out" while reviewing the Cuiyan exchange. A question joins the phrase to Danxia's burning of the wooden Buddha and asks why the monastery director's eyebrows fall out. The exact phrase is late and sparse, but its eyebrow-loss family is widely transmitted; the texts do not provide an anatomical explanation, and this entry adds none.

Senses.Note: One idiomatic referent covers the sampled uses. Pairings with “no dealings,” “sharing life and death,” speech/silence, and retreat opening are distinct contexts, not distinct objects or word classes. No second sense is created from competing readings of the image.

Senses.Explanation: The phrase reports the presiding figure raising the whisk where the assembly or questioner can see it. Huanglong Zuxin raises it after discussing the vine-and-tree saying, and Cian Jingyuan raises it in a hall address before uttering two sounds.

Senses.Explanation: To raise up and make prominent. Chan records make it a public teaching-seat verb: the named speaker proclaims the sect's purport, presents 'this matter' before the assembly, or is asked in an interview to present a cited event. One opening discourse pairs opening the hall with 'proclaiming the teaching of the school'; another records a whisk transmitted with the charge to present this matter before the human and heavenly assembly. A later discourse says that one sentence had already been presented before the listeners entered the gate.
